children: What happened?

A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after crude oil prices tumbled as renewed diplomatic talks between the United States and Iran eased concerns over potential Middle East supply disruptions.

Brent crude fell by more than 4%, while broader crude benchmarks dropped 3% following reports that negotiators convened in Doha to develop a framework for an agreement. For energy producers, crude prices directly dictate top-line revenue and operating margins. When geopolitical tensions flare across vital oil-producing regions, markets build in a risk premium, which is an additional cost priced into commodities to compensate for potential disruption risks.

Progress in diplomatic dialogue deflates this geopolitical risk premium, pushing oil prices lower. As the threat of imminent disruption to global supply routes recedes, investors quickly recalibrate expected cash flows for exploration and production firms, leading to widespread declines across the energy industry.
The stock market overreacts to news, and big price drops can present good opportunities to buy high-quality stocks.

Zooming in on Northern Oil and Gas (NOG)

Northern Oil and Gas’s shares are very volatile and have had 22 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 25 days ago when the stock gained 3.5% on the news that a Gulf tanker attack slowed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, while hurricane-driven production halts shut in Gulf of Mexico output, the Financial Times noted. The resulting supply squeeze lifted Brent crude above $104 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate to $92, according to CNBC. When global supplies face sudden restrictions, benchmark crude prices tend to spike, boosting revenue expectations and profitability for major oil and gas producers across the energy industry.

Northern Oil and Gas is up 19.2% since the beginning of the year, but at $26.24 per share, it is still trading 14.9% below its 52-week high of $30.82 from March 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Northern Oil and Gas’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $1,080.
